title: Diffusion into agar cubes
stem: Cubes of agar containing an alkaline pink indicator were placed in dilute acid. The time taken for each cube to become completely colourless (acid reaching the centre) was recorded for five cubes of each size.

data.caption: Mean time for agar cubes to become colourless (n = 5)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the 10 mm cube.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean rate at which acid penetrated the 20 mm cube, in mm min⁻¹.
markscheme: distance to centre = 10 mm (half the side length)
parts.notes: Award 1 mark for 20 / 52.0 = 0.38 mm min⁻¹ (full side length used).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between cube size and the time taken to become colourless.
markscheme: time increases as cube size increases
increase is more than proportional / non-linear: doubling side from 10 to 20 mm increases time 3.6 times
quoted data e.g. 4.0 min for 5 mm vs 52.0 min for 20 mm
SDs are small relative to differences so the trend is reliable

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how these results help to account for the limit on the size of cells.
markscheme: as size increases, surface area to volume ratio decreases
larger cubes take disproportionately longer for substances to reach the centre by diffusion
rate of exchange depends on surface area while demand depends on volume
in a large cell, oxygen / nutrients could not diffuse to the centre fast enough to meet metabolic needs
waste products / heat could not be removed fast enough
so cells divide / remain small / become flattened or elongated to keep a large SA:V

title: Ventilation in trained and untrained students
stem: Tidal volume and ventilation rate were measured with a spirometer in endurance-trained and untrained students, at rest and during 5 minutes of cycling at the same power output (n = 12 per group).

data.caption: Mean tidal volume and ventilation rate

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean volume of air ventilated per minute by untrained students during exercise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in volume ventilated per minute by trained students from rest to exercise.
markscheme: rest 0.62 × 11 = 6.82 dm³ min⁻¹ and exercise 2.60 × 32 = 83.2 dm³ min⁻¹
parts.notes: A common error is to give 1220 % (ratio × 100) instead of the percentage increase.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the breathing of trained and untrained students during exercise.
markscheme: both groups increase tidal volume and ventilation rate compared with rest
trained students have a larger tidal volume (2.60 vs 2.10 dm³)
trained students have a lower ventilation rate (32 vs 38 breaths min⁻¹)
trained students ventilate a larger volume per minute (83.2 vs 79.8 dm³ min⁻¹)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using the standard deviations, deduce whether the difference in tidal volume between the two groups during exercise is likely to be significant.
markscheme: untrained 1.80–2.40 dm³ and trained 2.25–2.95 dm³ (mean ± 1 SD)
the ranges overlap
so the difference may not be significant / a statistical test (e.g. t-test) is needed

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Suggest two variables that should be controlled in this investigation.
markscheme: age of students
sex / body mass / height of students
time since last meal / caffeine intake
duration and intensity / power output of exercise (same cycle settings)
room temperature / altitude
time of day / prior warm-up / rest period before measurement

title: Sarcomere length and muscle tension
stem: Single fibres from a frog leg muscle were stretched to different sarcomere lengths and then stimulated. The maximum tension produced is expressed as a percentage of the highest tension recorded (n = 6 fibres).

data.caption: Mean tension at different sarcomere lengths

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: In an electron micrograph a sarcomere of length 2.2 µm measures 33 mm. Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between sarcomere length and tension.
markscheme: tension increases from 1.6 to 2.2 µm
maximum tension (100 %) at 2.2 µm / between 2.0 and 2.2 µm
tension decreases at lengths above 2.2 µm
tension is almost zero at 3.6 µm (5 %)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain, using the sliding filament model, why tension falls as sarcomere length increases above 2.2 µm.
markscheme: tension depends on the number of cross-bridges formed between myosin heads and actin
as the sarcomere is stretched, overlap between actin and myosin filaments decreases
fewer myosin heads can bind to actin / fewer cross-bridges
less force is generated by power strokes / less sliding of actin towards the M line
at 3.6 µm there is (almost) no overlap so (almost) no tension

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest why tension is lower at a sarcomere length of 1.6 µm than at 2.2 µm.
markscheme: actin filaments from opposite ends overlap each other / collide in the middle
interfering with cross-bridge formation
myosin filaments are pushed against the Z lines / cannot shorten further
titin / elastic structures resist further compression

title: Plant zonation in a salt marsh
stem: A transect was run from the seaward edge of a salt marsh inland. At each distance, soil salinity was measured and percentage cover of two plant species, P and Q, was estimated in 10 quadrats.

data.caption: Soil salinity and mean percentage cover along the transect (n = 10 quadrats)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage change in mean cover of species P between 0 m and 40 m.
markscheme: −75 % / 75 % decrease (sign or 'decrease' required)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the distribution of species Q along the transect.
markscheme: absent at the seaward edge (0 m)
cover increases with distance from the sea
highest cover at 80 m (71 %)
largest increase between 20 and 40 m (6 % to 35 %)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the hypothesis that soil salinity determines the distribution of species P and Q.
markscheme: support: P cover is positively correlated with salinity / highest where salinity is 32 ppt
support: Q cover is negatively correlated with salinity / absent at highest salinity
support: Q's tolerance range appears not to include salinities above about 24–32 ppt
limitation: correlation does not prove causation
limitation: other factors vary with distance e.g. flooding frequency / waterlogging / soil oxygen
limitation: competition between P and Q may limit P inland (realized vs fundamental range)
limitation: only one transect / one marsh sampled
parts.notes: At least one supporting and one limiting point for full marks.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest one improvement to the method that would make the conclusion more reliable.
markscheme: use several transects / sample several marshes
grow P and Q in a controlled experiment at different salinities
measure other abiotic factors e.g. flooding / soil oxygen
repeat at different times of year

title: Carbohydrates and lipids as energy stores
stem: Plants and animals store energy in carbohydrates and lipids.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline how two glucose molecules are linked to form maltose.
markscheme: condensation reaction
water is removed / released
glycosidic bond formed
between carbon 1 of one glucose and carbon 4 of the other / 1,4 bond
both are α-glucose

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast the structure of starch (amylopectin), glycogen and cellulose.
markscheme: all are polysaccharides / polymers of glucose linked by glycosidic bonds
amylopectin and glycogen are made of α-glucose; cellulose of β-glucose
amylopectin and glycogen are branched (1,6 bonds); cellulose is unbranched
glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin
cellulose: alternate glucose units inverted / straight chains held in microfibrils by hydrogen bonds
amylopectin / glycogen are compact / coiled

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why animals use triglycerides rather than glycogen for long-term energy storage.
markscheme: triglycerides release about twice as much energy per gram
triglycerides are hydrophobic so are stored without water / glycogen is stored with water, adding mass
so lipid stores are lighter for the same energy, important for mobile animals
adipose tissue also gives thermal insulation / protection
glycogen is better for rapid release, so is used for short-term storage

title: Protein structure
stem: Proteins are polymers of amino acids whose function depends on their three-dimensional shape.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of different tripeptides that could be made from the 20 amino acids coded for in the genetic code.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how interactions between R groups determine the tertiary structure of a protein.
markscheme: tertiary structure is the folding of the polypeptide into a specific 3-D shape
hydrophobic R groups cluster in the interior away from water
hydrophilic / polar R groups are on the surface in contact with water
ionic bonds form between positively and negatively charged R groups
hydrogen bonds form between polar R groups
disulfide bonds (covalent) form between cysteine R groups
the sequence of amino acids (primary structure) determines where these interactions occur

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish between fibrous and globular proteins.
markscheme: fibrous are long and narrow / elongated; globular are rounded / spherical
fibrous are (usually) insoluble in water; globular are (usually) soluble
fibrous have structural roles e.g. collagen; globular have metabolic roles e.g. enzymes / insulin
fibrous often have repetitive amino acid sequences; globular have irregular sequences

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why many proteins lose their function at high temperatures.
markscheme: increased molecular vibration / kinetic energy breaks hydrogen bonds / ionic bonds
the protein denatures / the 3-D shape changes
e.g. active site no longer complementary to substrate
denaturation is usually irreversible
hydrophobic groups exposed so protein may become insoluble

title: Membranes and compartments
stem: Membranes surround cells and separate compartments within eukaryotic cells.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer in water.
markscheme: phospholipids are amphipathic
hydrophilic phosphate heads face the water on both sides
hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails face inwards away from water
this arrangement is the most stable / lowest energy state

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish between simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion across membranes.
markscheme: simple diffusion is directly through the phospholipid bilayer; facilitated diffusion is through channel / carrier proteins
simple diffusion for small / non-polar molecules e.g. O₂; facilitated for ions / polar molecules e.g. glucose
facilitated diffusion can be saturated / has a maximum rate; simple diffusion does not
facilitated diffusion is specific / can be gated
parts.notes: Reject 'facilitated diffusion uses ATP'; both are passive.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Outline an advantage of separating transcription from translation by the nuclear envelope.
markscheme: transcription occurs in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm
pre-mRNA can be modified / spliced before translation
introns removed so only mature mRNA is translated
prevents incorrect proteins being made / allows extra control of gene expression
mRNA leaves through nuclear pores

title: Transport in plants and animals
stem: Multicellular organisms need transport systems to move substances over long distances.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast the structure of arteries and veins.
markscheme: both have three layers / tunica externa, media and intima
both are lined with endothelium
arteries have thicker walls than veins (relative to lumen)
arteries have more smooth muscle and elastic fibres
veins have a wider lumen
veins have valves; arteries do not (except at base of aorta/pulmonary artery)
arteries are round in section; veins often flattened

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline how water moves up the xylem of a tall plant.
markscheme: transpiration: water evaporates from cell walls of spongy mesophyll and diffuses out through stomata
this creates tension / negative pressure in xylem
water is pulled up (from roots to leaves) by the tension
cohesion between water molecules due to hydrogen bonds keeps the column continuous
adhesion of water to the xylem walls / cellulose
xylem vessels are dead / hollow / lack end walls so offer little resistance
lignified walls prevent collapse under tension
passive process / no energy needed from the plant

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how the structure of capillaries is related to their function, including the formation and return of tissue fluid.
markscheme: capillary walls are one cell thick / endothelium only, so short diffusion distance
narrow lumen so red blood cells pass close to the wall / slow blood flow
extensive branching gives a large surface area for exchange
fenestrations / gaps between cells allow passage of fluid
at the arterial end, hydrostatic (blood) pressure is high
plasma is forced out to form tissue fluid
tissue fluid contains oxygen / glucose / ions but not large proteins / red blood cells
exchange of substances between tissue fluid and cells by diffusion
at the venous end, hydrostatic pressure is lower
water returns to the capillary by osmosis (plasma proteins lower water potential)
excess tissue fluid drains into lymph vessels and returns to the blood

title: Organelles and the secretory pathway
stem: Eukaryotic cells contain organelles whose structures are adapted to their functions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how the structure of a mitochondrion is adapted for aerobic respiration.
markscheme: double membrane / outer membrane separates mitochondrion from cytoplasm
small intermembrane space so proton gradient builds quickly
inner membrane folded into cristae to increase surface area
inner membrane contains electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase
matrix contains enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle
matrix contains 70S ribosomes / DNA to make some of its own proteins

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline the structure and function of the nuclear envelope.
markscheme: double membrane
outer membrane continuous with the rough ER
contains nuclear pores
pores allow mRNA / ribosome subunits to leave the nucleus
pores allow proteins e.g. histones / polymerases / nucleotides to enter
separates transcription in nucleus from translation in cytoplasm
envelope breaks down into vesicles during mitosis / meiosis

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how a protein that is secreted from a cell is synthesized, processed and released.
markscheme: gene transcribed to mRNA in the nucleus; mRNA exits through nuclear pores
translation begins on a free ribosome
signal sequence at the start of the polypeptide directs ribosome to the rough ER
polypeptide enters the lumen of the rough ER as it is synthesized
protein folds / is modified (e.g. glycosylation) in the ER
protein transported to the Golgi apparatus in vesicles budding from the ER
vesicles fuse with the cis face of the Golgi
protein further modified / sorted / packaged in the Golgi
secretory vesicles bud from the trans face of the Golgi
vesicles move to plasma membrane (along cytoskeleton)
vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane / exocytosis releases protein
ATP required for vesicle movement / exocytosis
parts.notes: Award marks for the correct sequence of organelles; reject 'the Golgi makes the protein'.

title: Adaptation, habitat and nutrition
stem: Organisms are adapted to the habitats in which they live and to the ways in which they obtain food.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline the modes of nutrition shown by organisms.
markscheme: autotrophs make their own carbon compounds from inorganic carbon (CO₂)
photoautotrophs use light energy / chemoautotrophs use energy from oxidation of inorganic chemicals
heterotrophs obtain carbon compounds from other organisms
holozoic nutrition: food ingested then digested internally
saprotrophs secrete digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorb products
mixotrophs can use both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition e.g. Euglena
named example of any mode

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe adaptations of herbivores for feeding on plants and adaptations of plants that resist herbivory.
markscheme: herbivore: grinding teeth / molars with ridges to break down cell walls
herbivore: mouthparts adapted for piercing / sucking e.g. aphids
herbivore: microbes in gut digest cellulose / long gut
herbivore: detoxification of plant toxins
plant: physical defences e.g. thorns / spines / hairs / tough leaves
plant: chemical defences e.g. toxins / alkaloids / tannins
plant: silica in leaves wears down teeth
parts.notes: For full marks both herbivore and plant adaptations must be described.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how abiotic factors and adaptations determine where a plant species can grow, using a named habitat as an example.
markscheme: each species has a range of tolerance for each abiotic factor
abiotic factors include temperature / water / light / salinity / soil pH / nutrients
species is found only where all factors are within its tolerance limits
named habitat e.g. sand dune / mangrove swamp / desert
sand dune: deep / extensive roots to reach water
sand dune: rolled leaves / sunken stomata / thick cuticle reduce water loss
mangrove: salt excreted from leaves / excluded at roots
mangrove: pneumatophores / aerial roots obtain oxygen in waterlogged mud
adaptations are inherited and result from natural selection
biotic factors e.g. competition may restrict species further
distribution can be investigated using transects / quadrats
climate (temperature and rainfall) determines biome / dominant vegetation
parts.notes: Award at most 4 marks if no named habitat with specific adaptations is given.
